Seminar Title:

Silicon Nanowire TOPCon Photovoltaics: Emitter Fabrication and Doping with Rear Tunnel-oxide Passivation

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Electrical Engineering

Speaker Name:

Sakti Prasanna Muduli ( Rollno : 521ee1013)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

EE401

Date and Time:

04 Nov 2026 11.00 AM

Contact:

Paresh G Kale

Abstract:

The demand for renewable energy is increasing, and photovoltaic (PV) energy is the primary source. Among commercialized terrestrial PV modules, c-Si cells are the most efficient choice. However, third-generation Si nanostructured PVs are still under development and are not yet competitive with commercial c-Si PVs. A Si-nanowire (SiNW) array is one of the Si nanostructures with significant characteristics &ndash improved photon absorption capability, bandgap tunability, and direct bandgap. The characteristics make the SiNW array a preferred emitter for Si PVs. Metal-assisted chemical etching (MACE) is the top-down, cost-effective chemical route for fabricating a vertical SiNW array using p-type wafers. The MACE controls the SiNW dimensions, thereby tuning the overall properties of the SiNW array. The work reveals that HF concentration and wafer resistivity are the most and least influential parameters for SiNW aspect ratio, respectively. An optimized SiNW array results in average reflectance and ultimate efficiency of 6.87% and 45.21%, respectively.
Spin-on doping with P2O5 as the phosphorus source for the SiNW array is a cost-effective method. The optimized P2O5 concentration of 5 mM yields an SiNW PV efficiency of 4.09% and a fill factor of 43.4%. The major issues with SiNW PV are rear-surface etching during MACE, phosphorus cluster formation during SOD, and the conventional dot-electrode pattern. The work solves the issues by using a modified MACE setup to eliminate rear etching, optimizing annealing at 900 &degC to dissolve phosphorus clusters, and employing a modified contact pattern to improve carrier collection. All the modification together improves the SiNW PV efficiency to 5.5%. Doping-induced defects are also analyzed using photoluminescence spectra.
The next possible way to further improve SiNW PV efficiency is to reduce rear surface recombination. For tunnel oxide passivation, the work first optimizes the nitric acid oxidation time to achieve an appropriate oxide thickness for tunneling and establishes the conduction mechanisms. Six minutes of oxidation results in ~1.4 nm of the tunnel layer containing suboxide and boron-related defects. For the p+ poly-Si layer deposition, a-Si and Al are sputtered, then annealed. The sequencing of the fabrication steps is managed to protect the SiNWs and the doping level during passivation layer deposition. It investigates the pinhole formation mechanism as a function of capping layer thickness and optimizes a 150 nm capping layer thickness, resulting in 6.7% efficiency.
Keywords: Passivation, Pinhole, Spin-on-doping, Sub-stoichiometric oxides, Tunneling
